title: UNICEF Democratic Republic of the Congo Humanitarian Situation Report No. 4 – Ebola Outbreak (Bundibugyo Virus), 30 September - ReliefWeb

analysis.time: As of 30 September 2026, the outbreak continued to expand geographically, with confirmed cases reported for the first time in Sud-Ubangi Province, bringing the number of affected provinces to seven. During September, an additional three health zones reported confirmed cases, increasing the total to 63 affected health zones. The publication date of the report is 27 October 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), specifically in Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, Bas-Uélé, and Sud-Ubangi provinces. Children under five bear the greatest burden, representing approximately 63.8 per cent of deaths among children aged 17 years and below. Women and girls represent approximately 53.4 per cent of reported confirmed cases.
analysis.event: An Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus, with confirmed cases and deaths reported in the DRC. The outbreak is now the largest ever recorded in the DRC and the second largest globally. UNICEF scaled up its multisectoral operations from 60 to 63 health zones, maintaining a presence in all 16 hotspots.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Between 1 and 30 September 2026, the DRC reported 2,050 additional confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) cases and 979 deaths. As of 30 September, cumulative confirmed cases had reached 8,300, including 4,018 deaths, corresponding to a case fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.4 per cent. Children aged 17 years and below account for approximately 27.4 per cent of confirmed cases and 37.6 per cent of reported deaths, indicating a disproportionate mortality burden among children.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Community-based surveillance was strengthened through the deployment of 3,469 additional community mobilizers. UNICEF requires US$ 113.5 million for its revised six-month response plan, with US$ 41 million mobilized as of 30 September, leaving a US$ 72.5 million funding gap.

analysis.brief_en: The UNICEF Humanitarian Situation Report No. 4 from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) highlights the ongoing Bundibugyo virus outbreak, which has expanded to seven provinces, including Sud-Ubangi. As of 30 September 2026, the DRC reported 2,050 additional confirmed cases and 979 deaths, bringing cumulative confirmed cases to 8,300 and deaths to 4,018, with a case fatality ratio of 48.4 per cent. Children under five account for 63.8 per cent of deaths among children aged 17 and below, and children aged 17 years and below represent 27.4 per cent of confirmed cases and 37.6 per cent of deaths. Women and girls make up 53.4 per cent of confirmed cases. The outbreak is the largest in the DRC and the second largest globally. UNICEF has scaled up operations to 63 health zones, maintaining a presence in all 16 hotspots. The organization has deployed 3,469 additional community mobilizers and expanded its response to include more than 590,000 litres of safe water, support to health facilities and schools, and decontamination capacity. UNICEF requires US$ 113.5 million for its revised six-month response plan, with US$ 41 million mobilized as of 30 September, leaving a US$ 72.5 million funding gap. Timely, flexible funding is urgently needed to sustain outbreak control and protect vulnerable populations, including children, in areas affected by conflict and displacement.

images © WHO South Sudan Credits+ The Ministry of Health of South Sudan, together with the National Public Health Institute (NPHI), and with support from the World Health Organization (WHO), the African Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), UNICEF, and other partners, conducted a five-day full-scale simulation exercise (SIMEX) from 19 to 24 October in Juba, Yei and Yambio to test the country’s readiness for Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD).
analysis.location_and_population: This area-based preparedness and readiness capacity building in the 15-priority counties focuses on early detection, timely notification, investigation, isolation, confirmation and containment (including contacts tracing) loop.
analysis.event: The simulation exercise is critical to test if these pillars can coherently work together at the right speed and technical accuracy to effectively contain any potential Ebola virus importation” Said Dr Ader Macar Aciek, Executive Director, National Public Health Institute (NPHI) “During the simulation exercise, the system will be activated including coordination, early detection, infection prevention and control, case management, risk communication and community engagement and safe/dignified burial.” This is the time to test our capabilities for BVD outbreak containment before we are confronted by the virus itself.” The SIMEX involved 10 participating sites (3 in Yambio, 3 in Yei and 4 in Juba), all supported by 9 facilitators, 9 evaluators and 9 observers.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Hypothetical scenarios of multiple suspected cases of Ebola virus disease (EVD) were used in the 10 simulation sites of three hubs.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The full scale simulation exercise also tested overall coordination and communication at national and sub-national levels and the linkages between the three levels of government; surveillance, and reporting of public health events; public health emergency operations Centre (PHEOC) activation, case management at designated isolation/treatment units; infection prevention and control practices; disinfection and waste management; risk communications; engagement of communities; finance and administration; operations support and logistics; movement of emergency supplies and equipment, Entry/exit screening of travelers, PHEOC ability to coordinate the multiple entities, collaboration of the various institutions among others.

analysis.brief_en: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued travel guidance for individuals returning to the United States from Ebola-affected areas, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), South Sudan, and Uganda. The guidance, published on October 22, 2026, outlines that travelers who have been in these regions within 21 days before departure will not be allowed to board flights to the U.S. and must remain outside the country for at least 21 days after leaving the affected areas. Additionally, those who have been in outbreak provinces in the DRC may face further local requirements. During entry screening, travelers will complete a questionnaire, have their temperature checked, and be observed for signs of illness. The CDC also enrolls travelers in automated text messages to remind them to monitor their health for 21 days post-travel. These measures are part of an official public health strategy to reduce the risk of Ebola virus disease importation. The CDC's guidance is based on confirmed evidence of Ebola virus disease outbreaks and is considered high confidence.

title: Ebola disease outbreak 2026: How MSF is responding - Doctors Without Borders

analysis.time: October 26, 2026; the outbreak has been ongoing since May 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), with MSF staff operating in Bunia, Ituri province.
analysis.event: An Ebola disease outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus is ongoing in DRC, with MSF providing treatment, setting up centers, and delivering supplies. The World Health Organization has declared it a public health emergency of international concern.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: More than 4,000 people have died since May 2026. Over 3,500 patients have been admitted to MSF treatment centers, with 580 survivors. The outbreak is the largest and fastest-spreading in DRC's history. Major gaps in diagnosis, surveillance, and community engagement continue to hinder control efforts.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: MSF has deployed over 2,800 staff to treat patients and set up facilities. The outbreak is under investigation, with challenges including conflict, insecurity, and a fragile health system. The response is ongoing and includes disease surveillance and community engagement.

analysis.brief_en: As of October 26, 2026, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is experiencing its largest and fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak ever recorded, with over 4,000 deaths since May. The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which has very few available medical tools. Doctors Without Borders (MSF) has deployed over 2,800 staff to treat patients, establish treatment centers, and deliver supplies to overwhelmed health facilities. The World Health Organization has declared the outbreak a public health emergency of international concern. MSF's response includes disease surveillance, rapid diagnosis, and community engagement to address fears and misinformation. Despite efforts, major gaps in diagnosis, surveillance, and contact tracing continue to challenge outbreak control. The response is further complicated by conflict, insecurity, and concurrent health needs in the region, especially with the onset of the rainy season. MSF's on-site laboratory at Elikiya treatment center processes samples quickly, reducing the time to results from two to three days to as little as one hour.

title: Large-scale meteorological patterns linked to Ebola virus outbreaks - News-Medical

analysis.time: The study analyzed data on 49 outbreaks in Africa between 1976 and 2025, with the latest report from the National Institute of Public Health (INSP) of the Democratic Republic of the Congo based on data collected through September 26, 2025. The research was conducted using data up to 2018 for model building and then validated from 2019 to 2025.
analysis.location_and_population: The study focused on Africa, particularly the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where the latest Ebola outbreak began in May 2025 and affected a significant population. The research also involved Central African wildlife and human interactions with it.
analysis.event: A study led by the University of Malaga and involving multiple institutions found that large-scale meteorological patterns, specifically teleconnections, are linked to the occurrence of Ebola virus outbreaks. The study is part of a broader effort to understand the transmission mechanisms of Ebola and predict new outbreaks.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The latest outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as of September 26, 2025, recorded more than 8,000 confirmed infections and 3,901 deaths, with a case fatality rate of nearly 50 percent. The study suggests that these teleconnections could serve as early warning signals for increased risk of outbreaks, with a predictive window of six to twelve months before potential events.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study has been published in the scientific journal Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment by Springer Nature. It is considered an initial step as a surveillance tool, but the predictive capacity is still limited and further research is needed before it can be used as an autonomous system.

analysis.brief_en: A study led by the University of Malaga, in collaboration with the Spanish Institute of Oceanography, Manchester Metropolitan University, and the Center for International Forestry Research, has found that large-scale meteorological patterns, known as teleconnections, are linked to the occurrence of Ebola virus outbreaks. The research analyzed data on 49 outbreaks in Africa between 1976 and 2025, comparing them with 26 climate oscillation indices. The latest report from the National Institute of Public Health (INSP) of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as of September 26, 2025, indicates over 8,000 confirmed infections and 3,901 deaths in the ongoing outbreak, with a case fatality rate of nearly 50 percent. The study highlights that these teleconnections may serve as early warning signals for increased risk of outbreaks, with a predictive window of six to twelve months. However, the researchers emphasize that the predictive capacity is still limited and further research is required before it can be considered an autonomous system. The findings could help activate preparedness measures when climate conditions suggest a higher likelihood of outbreaks, but they do not imply direct causation between distant climate indicators and the virus itself.
